title: Browser Storage: localStorage, sessionStorage, Cookies & IndexedDB
summary: Browsers offer several places to keep data on the client: **localStorage** (persistent, ~5MB, string-only), **sessionStorage** (per-tab, cleared on close), **cookies** (small, automatically sent to the server, with security attributes), and **IndexedDB** (a large async database). Choosing correctly depends on size, persistence, and whether the server needs the data.

subtopics.title: localStorage
subtopics.explanation: A synchronous key-value store scoped to an origin that PERSISTS across tabs, reloads, and browser restarts until explicitly cleared. It holds about 5MB and stores STRINGS ONLY, so objects must be serialized. The API is setItem(key, value), getItem(key), removeItem(key), clear(), and the length/key(i) helpers.

subtopics.title: sessionStorage
subtopics.explanation: Same API as localStorage but scoped to a single TAB (browsing context) and cleared when that tab closes. It is not shared between tabs even on the same origin. Use it for transient, tab-specific state like a multi-step form's progress or a one-visit flag.

subtopics.title: Strings only: JSON.stringify / JSON.parse
subtopics.explanation: Web Storage stores only strings, so to keep objects or arrays you serialize with JSON.stringify on write and JSON.parse on read. Always guard parsing (try/catch or a null check), because getItem returns null for missing keys and parsing null or malformed data throws.

subtopics.title: Cookies
subtopics.explanation: Small text values (~4KB each, limited per domain) that the browser AUTOMATICALLY sends to the server with every matching request. That makes them ideal for server-read session identifiers but a poor choice for bulk client data. They are read/written via document.cookie (a clunky string API) and support attributes controlling lifetime, path, domain, and security.

subtopics.title: Cookie security attributes
subtopics.explanation: HttpOnly hides the cookie from JavaScript (document.cookie can't read it), which mitigates token theft via XSS. Secure restricts the cookie to HTTPS. SameSite (Strict/Lax/None) controls whether the cookie is sent on cross-site requests, defending against CSRF. Sensitive tokens should be HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite, set by the server.

subtopics.title: IndexedDB (the big async store)
subtopics.explanation: A transactional, asynchronous NoSQL database in the browser that stores large amounts of structured data (well beyond 5MB) including objects, Blobs, and files, with indexes for querying. Its raw API is verbose and event/promise-based, so libraries like idb or Dexie are common. Use it for offline apps, caches, and large datasets — not tiny flags.

subtopics.title: Choosing the right store
subtopics.explanation: Use cookies only when the SERVER must read the value (sessions/auth) and keep them small and secured. Use localStorage for small, persistent, client-only preferences (theme, last tab). Use sessionStorage for transient per-tab state. Use IndexedDB for large or structured offline data. Match persistence, size, sync/async, and who reads it.
subtopics.example: // theme -> localStorage; auth token -> HttpOnly cookie; offline cache -> IndexedDB

subtopics.title: Security: XSS and tokens
subtopics.explanation: Anything in localStorage/sessionStorage is fully readable by any JavaScript on the page, so an XSS flaw can exfiltrate it — which is why auth tokens generally belong in HttpOnly cookies, not Web Storage. Never store secrets or PII in Web Storage, sanitize anything you render from storage, and treat stored data as untrusted on read.
subtopics.example: // avoid: localStorage.setItem('jwt', token)  prefer: HttpOnly cookie from server

foundations.overview: Client-side storage lets a web app remember data on the user's device. The platform offers complementary mechanisms differing in size, lifetime, synchronicity, and whether the data is shared with the server. Picking the right one is mostly about persistence needs, data size, and security.
foundations.formalDefinition: Web Storage (localStorage/sessionStorage) is a synchronous, origin-scoped, string key-value API. Cookies are small name-value pairs stored by the browser and transmitted in HTTP request headers, governed by attributes (Expires/Max-Age, Domain, Path, Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite). IndexedDB is an asynchronous, transactional object database for large structured data.
foundations.whyItMatters: Almost every app persists something client-side — preferences, drafts, carts, session state, offline data. Choosing the wrong store causes data loss, leaks, bloated requests, or security holes.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of cookies as a luggage tag that travels with every server request (small, server-visible), localStorage as a drawer in the user's house that stays until cleaned out, sessionStorage as a sticky note that's thrown away when the tab closes, and IndexedDB as a filing cabinet for big organized records.
foundations.browserPerspective: Web Storage is synchronous and lives on the main thread per origin; cookies are managed by the browser's network stack and attached to requests automatically; IndexedDB runs asynchronously so large reads/writes don't block rendering. Each is partitioned by origin (and increasingly by site for privacy).
foundations.realWorldUsage: Theme and language preferences in localStorage, multi-step form progress in sessionStorage, auth/session ids in HttpOnly cookies, and offline document caches or large media in IndexedDB.
foundations.businessImpact: Right-sized storage improves UX (remembered preferences, offline access) and protects users; storing tokens insecurely or bloating cookies harms security and performance, directly risking trust and conversions.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Understanding the trade-offs prevents leaks (tokens in localStorage), avoids surprising data loss (sessionStorage scope), and keeps requests lean (small cookies).
foundations.performanceImpact: Web Storage is synchronous, so large reads/writes can block the UI; cookies add weight to every request; IndexedDB is async and suited to large data without blocking. Keep cookies tiny and avoid huge synchronous Web Storage payloads.
commonUseCases: Persisting UI preferences (theme, language) in localStorage
Holding transient per-tab state (wizard progress) in sessionStorage
Server-read session/auth identifiers in secure cookies
Caching large/offline structured data in IndexedDB

commonMisconceptions.reality: It stores strings only; you must JSON.stringify on write and JSON.parse on read.

commonMisconceptions.myth: localStorage is a safe place for auth tokens.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Any script on the page can read it, so XSS can steal tokens; prefer HttpOnly cookies for credentials.

commonMisconceptions.myth: sessionStorage is shared across tabs like localStorage.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It's scoped to a single tab and cleared when that tab closes.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Cookies are just for client data like localStorage.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Cookies are sent to the server on every request and are limited (~4KB), so they're for small server-read values, not bulk client storage.

config.intro: Answer a few questions about your data to land on the right storage mechanism.

steps.name: Does the server need it?
steps.detail: If the backend must read it on each request (auth/session), use a cookie — and secure it.

steps.name: How sensitive is it?
steps.detail: Secrets/tokens should be HttpOnly + Secure cookies set by the server, never Web Storage.

steps.name: How long should it live?
steps.detail: Persist across sessions -> localStorage; only for this tab -> sessionStorage.

steps.name: How big / structured is it?
steps.detail: Small string-ish data fits Web Storage (~5MB); large or structured data belongs in IndexedDB.

steps.name: Sync or async?
steps.detail: Web Storage is synchronous (can block); IndexedDB is async and safe for large reads/writes.

steps.name: Serialize on write
steps.detail: For Web Storage, JSON.stringify objects on save and JSON.parse on load, guarding for null.

codeLab.title: Build a safe storage wrapper
codeLab.instructions: Implement a `store` object with get(key), set(key, value), and remove(key). set must JSON.stringify the value; get must JSON.parse it and return null for missing keys or parse errors. Verify behavior with console.log (do NOT rely on persistence across reloads).
codeLab.expectedOutput: Console logs the cart array and null for a missing key.
hints: get should return null when getItem returns null.
Wrap JSON.parse in try/catch to survive malformed data.

debuggingLab.title: Stored object reads back as '[object Object]'
debuggingLab.symptom: After saving a user object and reading it, the value is the string '[object Object]' instead of the original object.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Web Storage stores strings only. Passing an object to setItem implicitly calls String(object), which yields '[object Object]'. The structure is lost, so reading back gives a useless string with no properties.
commonMistakes: Forgetting that setItem coerces non-strings to strings.
Reading without JSON.parse even after stringifying.
Not guarding JSON.parse against null/malformed values.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Serialize on write and parse on read so the object round-trips correctly.

theory.question: Compare localStorage, sessionStorage, and cookies.
theory.directAnswer: All store data client-side but differ in lifetime, size, and reach. localStorage is ~5MB, string-only, and persists across tabs and restarts until cleared. sessionStorage shares the same API but is scoped to one tab and cleared when it closes. Cookies are tiny (~4KB), sent to the server with every matching request, and support security attributes — making them suited to small server-read values like session ids rather than bulk client data.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Three client storage mechanisms with different scopes and transport behavior.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Different needs — persistent prefs, transient tab state, and server-readable session data — require different tools.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Web Storage is a synchronous key-value API per origin; cookies are attached to HTTP requests by the browser based on their attributes.

theory.whyImportant: Choosing wrongly causes leaks (tokens in localStorage), data loss (sessionStorage scope), or bloated requests (large cookies).
theory.realWorldExample: Theme preference goes in localStorage; a multi-step form's progress in sessionStorage; the auth session id in an HttpOnly cookie.

nestedTopics.title: Strings only
nestedTopics.explanation: Web Storage requires JSON serialization for objects.

nestedTopics.title: Auto-sent cookies
nestedTopics.explanation: Cookies add weight to every request, so keep them small.

followUps.question: Which would you use for an auth token and why?
followUps.answer: An HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookie set by the server, so JavaScript can't read it (XSS resistance) and it's sent securely with requests.

theory.question: What do the HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite cookie attributes do?
theory.directAnswer: HttpOnly makes a cookie inaccessible to JavaScript (document.cookie can't read it), mitigating token theft via XSS. Secure restricts the cookie to HTTPS connections. SameSite (Strict/Lax/None) controls whether the cookie is sent on cross-site requests, which defends against CSRF. Sensitive cookies should combine HttpOnly, Secure, and an appropriate SameSite value, set by the server.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Security-relevant flags on the Set-Cookie header.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Cookies carry credentials, so the platform provides controls to limit exposure and cross-site transmission.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The browser enforces these flags: hiding HttpOnly cookies from scripts, only sending Secure cookies over TLS, and gating cross-site sends by SameSite.

theory.whyImportant: They are the front line against XSS token theft and CSRF, common interview and audit topics.
theory.realWorldExample: A login sets `Set-Cookie: session=...; HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite=Lax`.

nestedTopics.title: XSS vs CSRF
nestedTopics.explanation: HttpOnly addresses XSS theft; SameSite addresses CSRF.

nestedTopics.title: SameSite values
nestedTopics.explanation: Strict blocks cross-site sends; Lax allows top-level navigations; None requires Secure.

followUps.question: Why can't HttpOnly cookies be set from client JavaScript?
followUps.answer: HttpOnly is enforced by the browser and must be set via the server's Set-Cookie header; document.cookie can neither read nor set HttpOnly cookies.

scenario.question: Your app stores the JWT auth token in localStorage and a security review flags it. How do you respond and remediate?
scenario.directAnswer: localStorage is readable by any JavaScript on the page, so an XSS vulnerability could exfiltrate the token. I'd move the token to an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie set by the server so scripts can't read it, add CSRF protection (SameSite plus tokens for state-changing requests), tighten Content Security Policy and input sanitization to reduce XSS risk, and rotate any potentially exposed tokens. If a cookie isn't viable, I'd keep the token only in memory and use short-lived tokens with silent refresh.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A storage-security remediation for credential handling.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Web Storage offers no protection against script access, unlike HttpOnly cookies.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Moving the secret to an HttpOnly cookie removes it from the JS-reachable surface, shrinking the XSS blast radius.

scenario.whyImportant: Token theft leads to account takeover; this is a frequent real-world and interview security topic.

nestedTopics.title: XSS blast radius
nestedTopics.explanation: Anything JS can read, an injected script can steal.

nestedTopics.title: CSRF defense
nestedTopics.explanation: Cookies need SameSite and/or anti-CSRF tokens.

followUps.question: If you must keep a token client-side, what reduces risk?
followUps.answer: Keep it in memory (not Web Storage), use short expiry with refresh, and enforce a strict CSP plus rigorous output encoding.

coding.question: Implement a typed cache helper with set(key, value, ttlMs) and get(key) that expires entries using localStorage.
coding.thoughtProcess: Web Storage has no built-in TTL, so I'll store a wrapper object { value, expiresAt } as JSON. On get, I parse, compare expiresAt to now, and return null (removing the entry) if expired. I'll guard parsing and null reads. Demonstrating with logs avoids relying on real persistence.
coding.lineByLine: set wraps the value with an absolute expiresAt timestamp and JSON.stringifies it. get parses safely (returning null on missing/invalid data), checks whether now has passed expiresAt, removes and returns null if expired, otherwise returns the original value. This adds TTL semantics on top of string-only Web Storage.
coding.spaceComplexity: O(n) in the size of the serialized value.

alternativeApproaches.title: IndexedDB for large/async caches
alternativeApproaches.explanation: For big or many entries, use IndexedDB so reads/writes are async and don't block the main thread.
alternativeApproaches.code: // open('cacheDB'), put { key, value, expiresAt } in a store with an index

followUps.question: Why store an absolute expiresAt instead of a duration?
followUps.answer: An absolute timestamp lets get decide expiry purely from the current time, with no need to track when it was written separately.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Apps layer storage by purpose: HttpOnly cookies for credentials, localStorage for small persistent client preferences, sessionStorage for tab-scoped flows, and IndexedDB for offline caches and large datasets. A thin storage abstraction centralizes serialization, TTL, and error handling.
productionDeepDive.performance: Web Storage is synchronous and blocks the main thread, so avoid large payloads; cookies add bytes to every request, so keep them minimal; IndexedDB is asynchronous and appropriate for large reads/writes without jank.
productionDeepDive.security: Never store secrets/PII in Web Storage (XSS-readable); use HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookies for tokens, sanitize anything rendered from storage, and treat stored data as untrusted input on read. A strict CSP reduces the XSS that would compromise client storage.
productionDeepDive.scaling: As stored data grows or needs structure/offline querying, migrate from Web Storage to IndexedDB; keep cookies small to avoid request bloat at high traffic.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: A single wrapper for get/set/remove with JSON handling, namespacing, and versioned keys prevents scattered, fragile storage calls and eases migrations.
productionDeepDive.observability: Chrome DevTools' Application panel inspects localStorage, sessionStorage, cookies, and IndexedDB; quota errors (QuotaExceededError) and parse failures should be logged and handled gracefully.

caseStudies.problem: Needed reliable offline access to large structured data.
caseStudies.solution: Use IndexedDB (often via idb/Dexie) for the data layer with cookies for auth and localStorage for small prefs.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: More complex async data layer vs. robust offline capability and proper security separation.
caseStudies.lessons: Match each datum to the storage whose lifetime, size, and security fit it.

keyTakeaways: localStorage persists across sessions (~5MB, string-only); sessionStorage shares the API but is per-tab and cleared on close.
Web Storage stores strings only — JSON.stringify on write and JSON.parse (guarded) on read for objects.
Cookies are small (~4KB) and auto-sent to the server; secure them with HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite for sessions/auth.
Use IndexedDB for large, structured, or offline data — it's asynchronous and scales well beyond Web Storage.
Never keep tokens or secrets in Web Storage (XSS-readable); choose storage by who reads it, size, persistence, and security.
